source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist: What Does the Scientific Method Buy an LLM Agent?
finding: An LLM scientist loop (hypothesis, prediction, code, test, reconciliation) is paired with a separate Kuhn agent that injects a paradigm-shifting reframing when progress plateaus. This is the closest direct use of Kuhn's idea inside an agent loop.
numbers: On DNA motif discovery the framework produced DALE, which beat STREME on 132 ENCODE transcription factors and ran about 11 times faster. Kuhn agent phase: 63 runs, 33.5M tokens, 3 days (whole project 229.0M tokens, 2,151 runs, 26 active days).
limits: The author himself says the ablation found the Kuhn structure not load-bearing against a simple control statement. One domain, one author, one benchmark.
agent_relevance: A Kuhn-style reframe stage (O8) costs real tokens and must be tested against a plain control before it stays in the schema.

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist: What Does the Scientific Method Buy an LLM Agent?
finding: Design of the Kuhn trigger. It fires after a set number of consecutive non-improving iterations (an impasse trigger). It gets the task text but NOT the history file or built-up artifacts, plus a random paradigm-shifting conjecture paired with a random cross-disciplinary inspiration (example: architecture, load-bearing analysis).
numbers: Trigger = N consecutive non-improving iterations (configurable). Kuhn side-agents made approximately zero web-search calls; external research calls averaged 3 to 14 per run (1% of tool calls).
quote: LLMs proceed from their own context
limits: Mechanism is described 'to allow comparison'. The conjectures are random, not derived from the anomalies seen.
agent_relevance: Matches our idea of clearing context to escape fixation. The useful part may be the cleared context, not the random analogy (untested here).

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist: What Does the Scientific Method Buy an LLM Agent?
finding: Preregistered ablation of ten loop variants against bandit nulls (independent one-shot pulls from the same model and prompt). The full scaffold scored BELOW blind sampling. The registered assumption that ablations cannot beat the full scaffold was falsified.
numbers: n=10 runs per arm, 15 counted iterations. Top-run mean: full scaffold B 0.8027; no scaffold G 0.8612; floor prompt L 0.8906 (best, +0.1159 gain); one-shot null E[best-of-15] 0.8463 (H) and 0.8455 (HG). 7 of 10 arms fail to beat the bandit. B used 111.4M tokens per run vs 15M for fifteen fresh pulls (7-8x).
limits: Proxy metric on 15 synthetic TFs; low pairwise power at n=10; twelve amendments and a post-hoc relabeled family are disclosed.
agent_relevance: Heavy scaffolds that reframe and reconcile can lose to best-of-N on equal budget. Our schema must be scored against a best-of-N arm.

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist: What Does the Scientific Method Buy an LLM Agent?
finding: Token forensics of why the full scaffold lost: its cost is context, not reasoning. Selection among one-shot draws also Goodharts without iteration.
numbers: Cache re-reads were 2.5x the counted tokens; output 4% of spend; explicit reasoning 2.5%. Of 64 evaluated Phase 2 iterations, 17 improved the best (26.6%). First DALE gain at run 25 (about 4.9M tokens); best score 0.843 at run 52 (about 10.2M tokens); 448 later runs found no more.
limits: Single domain.
agent_relevance: Impasse-triggered stages should keep context short; long histories are the cost driver.

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist: What Does the Scientific Method Buy an LLM Agent?
finding: Light prompts beat heavy ones: the floor prompt was the best arm, and replacing per-instance diagnostics with a scalar score cost points.
numbers: Top-run mean: L floor prompt 0.8906; F no reconciliation 0.8569; D no predictions/blockers 0.8478; C scalar feedback 0.8428; I forced worksheet 0.8179.
limits: n=10 per arm; wide spread; arms added by amendment.
agent_relevance: Keep each operator light until it is shown to pay.

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist: What Does the Scientific Method Buy an LLM Agent?
finding: The Kuhn stage was run as a phase on its own during development but was not isolated as a separate arm in the ablation table, so its marginal effect is unmeasured.
numbers: Table 1 compute: initial search 1,588 runs 97.6M tokens; Kuhn agent 63 runs 33.5M; full-framework search 500 runs 97.9M.
limits: No Kuhn-only arm.
agent_relevance: No evidence yet that a reframing agent pays. We need our own single-factor test.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without external feedback, asking a model to review and revise its own answer does not help and often hurts. This is the key negative result for any 'notice the anomaly yourself' step.
numbers: Intrinsic self-correction, rounds 1 / 3 / 5 calls. GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 / 75.1 / 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 / 38.1 / 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 / 25.0 / 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 / 91.5 / 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 / 79.5 / 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 / 49.0 / 43.0.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback
limits: Reasoning tasks only, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2.
agent_relevance: An impasse or anomaly signal must come from outside the model (test result, tool output, verifier), not from the model's own judgement of its answer.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Why intrinsic revision fails: the model cannot judge if its own reasoning is correct, so it flips right answers to wrong more often than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 on GSM8K keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time after two rounds. GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo keep initial answers more often. CommonSenseQA: false options look relevant, so the model changes its answer much more often.
limits: Figure-level counts not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gate any revise operator on external evidence. Default to keep the current answer when no new evidence arrives.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Earlier reported self-correction gains came from using ground-truth labels to decide when to stop. With oracle labels the same models look much better.
numbers: Oracle table, GPT-4: HotpotQA 29.0 standard to 59.0 with oracle self-correct; GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5 (GPT-4 rows). Without the oracle (Table 3) GPT-4 HotpotQA falls from 49.0 to 43.0 by 5 calls.
limits: Table layout in the PDF text is hard to align by row; the HotpotQA oracle figure is the cleanest reading.
agent_relevance: Any claimed revise gain must be checked with an oracle-free arm and an equal-call self-consistency arm.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: Critical survey. (1) No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from a prompted LLM, except tasks unusually suited to it. (2) Self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists. (3) Large-scale fine-tuning can enable it. The bottleneck is feedback generation.
numbers: Qualitative; offers a checklist for fair self-correction experiments.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Narrative survey with no pooled effect size.
agent_relevance: Build the anomaly detector from execution results and verifiers, not from self-critique.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: After a failed trial with an external signal, the agent writes a verbal reflection into memory and retries. A working impasse-then-revise loop with an outside trigger.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. Gains over strong baselines: +22% on AlfWorld (134 environments, 12 iterative steps), +20% on HotPotQA, +11% on coding tasks (as the paper states).
limits: Needs an environment signal (test results, binary reward). Later critiques (Huang 2024) show the benefit shrinks without it.
agent_relevance: Template for O8: outside failure signal, short written diagnosis, retry with diagnosis in context.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
finding: An 'aha moment' appears during RL: a sudden increase in the use of 'wait' while the model rethinks and tries alternative solutions. Nearest machine analogue of insight after impasse.
numbers: AIME 2024 pass@1 of R1-Zero rose from 15.6% to 77.9% during RL; response length grew to thousands of tokens.
quote: a sudden increase in the use of the word "wait" during reflections
limits: The aha claim rests on one transcript (Table 2) and a rise in the frequency of 'wait'. The paper does not test that it causes the gain.
agent_relevance: Cheap reflect-and-recheck behaviour already exists in reasoning models. A scaffold need not add it from scratch.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models
finding: Reasoning models show three regimes. On easy puzzles they find the answer early and keep exploring wrong ones (overthinking). On medium ones correct answers come only after wrong paths. Past a threshold they fixate on early wrong attempts and accuracy collapses to near zero.
numbers: Controlled puzzles with tunable complexity; thinking tokens fall as complexity rises past the collapse point; near-zero accuracy beyond a model-specific complexity.
limits: Puzzles, not theory change. Rebuttals on output-length limits exist; I did not open them.
agent_relevance: Fixation on an early wrong frame is measured. At the hard end the model does not reframe by itself, so reframing must be forced.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: A Virtual Environment for Developing and Evaluating Automated Scientific Discovery Agents
finding: 120 simulated discovery tasks (8 topics x 3 difficulties) needing hypothesis, experiment, analysis and action. Baseline agents struggle; human scientists do far better.
numbers: Human mean completion 66% (11 of 16 tasks over 60%), knowledge 55%. Best agent (ReAct, GPT-4o) completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks. Hypothesizer found 34% of gold knowledge on easy and 8% on challenge. Unit-test sub-skills: completion in the 60%+ range.
limits: GPT-4o only. Not an explicit Kuhn test; some tasks hold an anomalous item.
agent_relevance: Agents manage single steps but fail end-to-end revision of explanations. A good place to test the reframe operator.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models with Hypothesis Refinement
finding: Iterative propose-test-refine of rules with a symbolic interpreter makes GPT-4 a strong hypothesis proposer but a weak applier of its own rules.
numbers: ACRE task accuracy: direct IO 28.0; self-consistency N=5 29.0; self-refine 32.0; refinement T=1,N=1 45.0; T=3,N=5 59.0. MiniSCAN task accuracy 0.0 (IO) vs 46.0 (T=3,N=1). MiniARC task accuracy 13.8 (IO) vs 14.6 (T=3,N=5).
limits: Gains need a task-specific interpreter to filter rules. Without it, self-refine adds only 4 points on ACRE. GPT-4 only (gpt-4-0613).
agent_relevance: Hypothesis revision works when a program checks it. The checker carries the gain.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models with Hypothesis Refinement
finding: Brittle to anomalous data: with noisy exemplars the model does substantially worse even with one noisy example, and worse still as noise grows.
numbers: List Functions, 8 exemplars; 12.5%, 25% and 50% of exemplars corrupted; accuracy fell at each step. An instruction to expect noise reduced but did not remove the drop.
limits: Exact values are in a figure not readable from text.
agent_relevance: Models do not separate 'noise' from 'signal that breaks my rule'. The scaffold should count and decide.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models
finding: Generate several abstract hypotheses in words, implement each as a program, run on the examples. Filtering by an LLM summary or a human pick helps.
numbers: ARC 100-problem subset: direct prompting 17%; program form 23%; plus LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%; human-selected 33%. Of 49 tasks with selected hypotheses, 33 (67%) gave a correct program. SyGuS 94.3% of tasks.
limits: GPT-4; random 100-task subset; human selection adds a hand.
agent_relevance: Several rival frames, each tested by running code, beat one-shot answers. Supports a rival-hypothesis step.

source: Agarwal, Majumder et al. (2025) AutoDiscovery: Open-ended Scientific Discovery via Bayesian Surprise
finding: Uses the LLM's change of belief (prior to posterior after experiments) as a reward in tree search. This turns the Kuhnian anomaly into a number that drives exploration.
numbers: 21 datasets; 5-29% more discoveries judged surprising than competitors at fixed budget. Human study over 500+ hypotheses: 67% of surprising discoveries also surprised domain experts; Bayesian surprise correlates 0.67 with human surprisal (95% CI 0.63-0.71, 10,000 bootstraps); next best reward 0.46 points lower. Experiment validity above 95%.
limits: Belief is elicited by sampling the same LLM, so prior contamination is possible; datasets are tabular.
agent_relevance: A concrete anomaly detector: sample belief before and after evidence; trigger reframing when it shifts across the decision threshold.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of Large Language Models Reasoning
finding: Belief-R tests whether models drop a prior conclusion when a new premise undermines it. 30 models struggled; the ones good at updating often failed to keep correct beliefs, so there is a trade-off.
numbers: BREU = mean of belief-update accuracy (BU) and belief-maintain accuracy (BM). GPT-4-Turbo direct: BU 19.65%, BM 82.69%, BREU 51.17. Llama-3 70B direct: BU 10.99%, BM 92.09%, BREU 51.54. Best models at most about 50% BREU. CoT and problem-solving prompts moved scores only a point or two.
limits: Text defeasible-logic items (Tweety style), not scientific anomalies.
agent_relevance: Models over-maintain beliefs. Updating needs an explicit challenge step, and over-updating must be checked too.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring the Capabilities and Limitations of Language Models Through Counterfactual Tasks
finding: Changing a familiar rule system (base-9 arithmetic, 1-based indexing, altered chess rules) leaves the reasoning procedure intact, but models do much worse. Success on default conditions is not evidence of a general ability.
numbers: 11 task suites; GPT-4 and others drop on counterfactual variants and the drop correlates with default-task skill. Zero-shot chain of thought helps unevenly.
quote: small variations on the default instantiations of tasks are challenging for models
limits: Exact accuracies sit in figures I did not extract.
agent_relevance: Machine form of 'working under a changed framework'. Write the new rules out explicitly when the agent changes frame.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: Benchmarking Progress in Automated Experimental Design and Model Discovery
finding: 10 environments test whether an LLM can propose a model, run experiments and revise it. All approaches struggle. 32B beats 7B; closed models beat open ones. Explanations passed to a novice help, but less than running the experiments.
numbers: 10 environments; metrics are expected information gain and standardized prediction error; gpt-4o novice. Population growth gives negative standardized error (good); hyperbolic discounting stays poor after experiments.
limits: Probabilistic simulators, not historical revolutions.
agent_relevance: A way to score whether a revised explanation truly predicts better.

source: Zhu & Rzeszotarski (2025) What We Talk About When We Talk About LMs: Implicit Paradigm Shifts and the Ship of Language Models
finding: Conceptual change in NLP itself: the term 'language model' is retrofitted over time, not replaced. A Kuhn-style study built on the ACL Anthology.
numbers: Dataset of 7,650 papers; LM-related papers 35% at ACL 2020; model-name composition similarity between venues falls from 71-86% (adjacent) to 45-56% over two years and 24-31% over three.
limits: Studies a term of art, not model behaviour.
agent_relevance: Word meaning drifts, so the agent should pin its definitions when it changes frame.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence (Behavioral and Brain Sciences)
finding: ECHO, a connectionist model of explanatory coherence, was applied to Lavoisier's argument for oxygen against phlogiston, to Darwin, and to legal reasoning. A hypothesis is accepted if it coheres better overall than rivals.
numbers: Seven principles; no activation data seen (abstract page only).
limits: Full text paywalled. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: A cheap coherence ranker over rival explanations could serve as the accept/reject step after a reframe.

source: Thagard coherence as constraint satisfaction (Wikipedia summary)
finding: Thagard and Verbeurgt formalised coherence as constraint satisfaction: weighted positive and negative constraints between elements, and the aim is to split elements into accepted and rejected sets that satisfy as much weight as possible.
numbers: No simulation counts on the page; it only lists the 1990 paper 'The Conceptual Structure of the Chemical Revolution'.
limits: Secondary, short page.
agent_relevance: Frame the choice among frames as constraint satisfaction.

source: Kulkarni & Simon (1988) The Processes of Scientific Discovery: The Strategy of Experimentation (KEKADA)
finding: KEKADA simulated Krebs's discovery of the urea (ornithine) cycle and reacts to surprising results by focusing follow-up experiments on the surprise. An early AI system with an anomaly-driven strategy.
numbers: Not retrieved. The DOI is confirmed by Crossref; the full text was blocked (403) and the DTIC copy returned an HTML page.
limits: Cited from the Crossref record and prior knowledge; not read.
agent_relevance: Original design for 'surprise leads to a focused follow-up experiment'.
